For causal evaluation, this creates a difficult spatiotemporal problem: intermittent policy updates create path-level treatments, and because spillover depends on neighboring treatment paths along with the focal-unit's own history, controlling time-varying confounding requires high-dimensional, multimodal information from both sources. To address this challenge, we develop a neural spatiotemporal spillover framework that extends potential-outcome causal analysis to networked policy-systems with unit-level effects and structured interference. The framework indexes each unit's potential outcomes through own-treatment and neighborhood spillover-exposure paths, yielding direct, spillover, and total effects. We introduce an LSTM-based representation-learning encoder that integrates each unit's own and neighborhood histories into compact sequential summaries for downstream modeling and causal estimation. These summaries feed a self-normalized kernel inverse-probability-weighting estimator for continuous spillover exposure. Beyond theoretical guarantees, simulations show improved performance over outcome-regression baselines; in a practically motivated county-level COVID-19 policy study, the framework finds both business-and-economic restrictions and education-and-childcare policies associated with lower subsequent case burden, with larger estimates for business-and-economic restrictions. Overall, it provides a scalable, policy-interpretable framework for evaluating unit-level effects in high-dimensional, multimodal spatiotemporal systems when interventions spill over across space and time.

title: Small area learning
abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop standard and cross-fitted estimators for low-complexity and flexible learners, unifying synthetic, model-based, and fully residual-corrected estimation. For area means, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality and provide variance estimators and confidence intervals. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals a bias--variance trade-off: partial residual correction can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to working-model misspecification, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34\%--49\% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. An empirical application favours a cross-fitted estimator using a flexible learner under the chosen validation criterion. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.

title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
abstract: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

title: Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle
abstract: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $\Omega((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

title: Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
abstract: We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.

title: Jensen-Bregman split Gibbs sampling
authors: Mame Diarra Fall and Eric Barat
abstract: Split Gibbs sampling (SGS) is a versatile tool to sample from complex posterior distributions, such as those arising in imaging inverse problems. However, existing SGS instances are limited to quadratic variable couplings, restricting their applicability to Gaussian likelihoods. This letter genearalizes SGS to non-Euclidean geometry by introducing a coupling kernel defined through a Jensen-Bregman divergence. This framework not only enables posterior sampling in these settings but also unifies several \emph{ad hoc} sampling schemes from the literature under a principled theoretical foundation.

title: Fair Allocation with Dichotomous Preferences over Item Complements
abstract: We study the problem of fair allocation when agents have dichotomous submodular preferences over groups of, rather than individual, items. These preferences naturally extend existing models, and have a natural interpretation in settings such as course allocation. We show that this seemingly minor extension results in computational intractability barriers: computing a utilitarian or Nash-optimal allocation with item complements is NP-hard. However, when agents' complementary bundles have size at most $k$, there exist poly-time algorithms that compute $\frac1k$-$\texttt{maxUSW}$ allocations and approximate Nash-welfare-maximizing allocations. While PO+EF-1 allocations may not exist in the complementary preference setting, it is possible to compute $\frac1{k+1}$-approximately $\texttt{maxUSW}$ EF-X allocations in polynomial time; furthermore, these allocations offer each agent $i$ a utility of at least $\frac{\texttt{MMS}_i - k}{k+1 + \frac1n}$, where $\texttt{MMS}_i$ is agent $i$'s maximin share guarantee. While the standard dichotomous binary submodular setting admits simple sequential techniques for computing fair and efficient allocations, our results for the complements setting require more complex tools from combinatorial optimization.

title: Inference on the Value of Policy Improvement in Adaptive Experiments
abstract: In this paper, we develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data. This value, which is defined as the gap between the value of the best treatment policy in a class and that of a baseline policy, gauges whether or not it is worth deploying a personalized treatment policy. Building an estimator for the VPI is naturally more difficult than estimating the value of a fixed policy. This is because, in addition to contending with the correlated data and decaying propensities associated with adaptive experiments, any estimator must also handle the non-regularity, or lack of pathwise differentiability, of the underlying estimand when the optimal policy is non-unique. Our proposed estimator works by sequentially fitting a weighted empirical welfare maximizing policy on historical data and then evaluating it using inverse propensity weighting on future samples. We neither assume that the optimal policy is unique nor make a margin assumption on the underlying heterogeneous treatment effects. A key difficulty in analyzing our estimator is showing that the regret incurred through policy learning is asymptotically smaller than the standard error of the estimator. We accomplish this by showing faster regret rates for policy learning under decaying propensities, which may be of independent interest. We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.

title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
abstract: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the project's quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. A natural benchmark uses the review only after it arrives, to update beliefs and improve the second-period allocation. The optimal mechanism instead frontloads the review's information value: it also uses the review as an incentive device to elicit truthful reporting up front, thereby strictly improving the principal's first-period expected payoff. In the optimal mechanism, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but face larger cuts after a bad review, leaving them with less funding than lower-quality projects. A good review increases funding, but the resulting allocation need not preserve the initial ranking of projects and eventually declines with quality.

title: The LR2 Lifetime Distribution: Rate Crossing, Reliability Properties, and Estimation
abstract: We study the LR2 one-parameter lifetime distribution obtained by mixing an exponential component of rate $\theta/2$ and a gamma component with shape four and rate $\theta^2$. The exponential mixing probability is $\theta^2/(1+\theta^2)$ for $\theta>0$. We derive the density, survival function, moments, transforms, truncated moments, quantiles, order-statistic distributions, mean residual life, and stress--strength reliability. Identifiability follows from the density at the origin, and strict monotonicity of the mean yields a unique moment estimator. A complete density-turning-point criterion and analytic initial and tail hazard expansions clarify the possible shapes. The component rates cross at one half. The hazard decreases initially for every positive parameter and eventually increases in the gamma-dominated regime; it eventually decreases in the exponential-dominated regime. We develop likelihood estimation, observed information, constrained expectation--maximization, spacing estimation, and inference under regularity conditions, and state the likelihood for independent right censoring. A reproducible Monte Carlo study with eight settings and 4,000 generated samples compares likelihood and moment estimation and evaluates log-scale confidence intervals. The analysis distinguishes mathematical properties from empirical validation and explains the restrictions associated with a fixed working time unit.

title: Adaptive Robust Confidence Sets in High Dimensions
authors: Ilias Diakonikolas and Chao Gao and Daniel M. Kane and Yuetian Luo
abstract: We study adaptive confidence sets for mean vectors of multivariate Gaussians with identity covariance under Huber contamination when the contamination proportion is unknown. We show that an information-theoretically optimal adaptive confidence set can be constructed by simultaneously quantifying uncertainty across all one-dimensional projections. The resulting confidence set achieves the optimal diameter and reveals a substantial adaptation cost compared with the minimax estimation error. Although statistically optimal, this construction is computationally infeasible. We establish a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound showing that achieving diameter $O(m^{-1/2})$ requires either exponentially many queries or query tolerance $d^{-\Omega(m)}$. Thus, in contrast to robust mean estimation, adaptation to the unknown contamination proportion incurs both a statistical cost and a computational barrier within the SQ framework. Finally, we give a low-degree moment-matching algorithm that constructs an adaptive confidence set using $d^{O(m)}$ samples and time. Its diameter bound contains an additional $O(m^{-1/2})$ term beyond the information-theoretic rate, matching the dependence on $m$ in the SQ lower bound. Together, these results characterize the statistical limits of adaptive robust confidence sets under Huber contamination and quantify a computational barrier within the SQ framework.

title: Uncertainty in Compound Decisions
abstract: Researchers and policymakers frequently make a large number of decisions simultaneously over many units using noisy estimates of unit-level effects. Researchers often assume that unit-level effects are drawn from a common effect distribution, allowing for optimal decision-making. In applications, however, this effect distribution is unknown to the econometrician, introducing uncertainty in the ultimate decision-making problem. This paper considers the problem of quantifying this uncertainty. For instance, researchers may seek to understand how an oracle decision maker with knowledge of the effect distribution would compare different feasible decisions, or understand which decisions an oracle would plausibly make. Analyzing these questions from the perspective of an oracle decision maker involves comparing the conditional means of unit-level effects given estimates thereof, suggesting a sufficient inferential objective of uniform coverage of these conditional means. Based on an equivalence between uniform coverage of conditional means and multiple testing, I develop methods that satisfy this coverage. Finally, I consider an application to the problem of identifying high-economic-mobility neighborhoods. My methods sharpen inference relative to existing methods and identify units that can be confidently included in oracle selections.

title: One Goodness-of-Fit Test Is Not Enough: Error-Controlled Localization of Misfit in Logistic Risk Models
abstract: A goodness-of-fit test tells whether a logistic risk model fits, but the analyst also needs to know what is wrong: an overall risk that is too high is repaired by updating the intercept, risks that are too extreme by recalibration, a curved relation between score and risk by a flexible recalibration, and misfit within groups of patients only by revising the model. We split any misfit into these four parts, which are orthogonal and match the calibration hierarchy. Each part gets a group of score tests that sees that part only, and the failing parts are named by closed testing. In external validation, in large samples and for small departures, a part is wrongly named with probability at most the chosen level, and the highest part named points to the lightest update that removes the misfit. Checking a model on its development data never sees an error in the overall risk or the calibration slope, and with binary or skewed covariates it can mistake misfit within patient groups for a curved link. External validation sees all four parts, for any prediction model. In simulations it kept its error rate when the model was right and for small departures, and usually pointed to the right update. On intensive-care data its verdicts for one model differed in-sample, on similar patients and after transport.

title: Thompson Sampling for Learning in Zero-Sum Games
abstract: Thompson sampling (TS) achieves logarithmic and asymptotically optimal regret in classical stochastic bandits, but its behavior in multi-agent learning remains less understood. We study TS in an unknown finite two-player zero-sum matrix game with Gaussian bandit feedback. Under centralized self-play, TS samples a single payoff matrix from the posterior and plays a Nash equilibrium of the sampled game. For every fixed zero-sum game with a unique Nash equilibrium, we show that the expected cumulative duality gap is $O(\sqrt T)$. The rate improves to $O(\log T)$ for pure equilibria. We then identify the exact coefficient of the $\sqrt T$ term, which depends only on the equilibrium strategies and the noise level. We also establish a minimax lower bound matching the square-root dependence on $T$ and an instance-dependent lower bound matching the logarithmic dependence on $T$ for a class of games with a unique pure equilibrium. Experiments support the predicted rates and coefficient.

title: Rank-based Model Average Estimator for Average Treatment Effects
abstract: Model averaging emerges as an attractive ensemble technique that strategically synthesizes all available information from potential candidate models to enhance estimation accuracy. Despite of having been widely practiced in various areas in biostatistics and economics, its application to causal inference is rather limited. We propose to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) by forming the weighted combination of the robust rank-based estimators obtained from a series of candidate models, where the model weights, selected via the growing window cross-validation, dynamically adjust the importance of candidate models. The proposed robust rank-based model averaging ({\sf RRMA}) is not only robust to handle potential outliers and heavy-tailed error distributions but also capable to reduce the risk of model mis-specification and enhance the flexibility and the accuracy of estimation. Theoretically, we establish the desirable asymptotic properties of {\sf RRMA}, including the asymptotic optimality, consistency and asymptotic distribution. Moreover, motivated by the asymptotic distribution of {\sf RRMA}, an easy-to-implement confidence interval is also developed for the ATE. Simulation experiments and an empirical application demonstrate the superiority of {\sf RRMA} over existing competitors in estimation accuracy, coverage probabilities and widths of confidence intervals.

title: Identifying and Measuring Treatment-Effect Heterogeneity across Sites through Within-Site Randomization
abstract: Parallel cluster-randomized trials can identify mean effects by site characteristics and risk differences between fixed predictors, while leaving residual heterogeneity and absolute prediction risk (mean squared error of site-effect predictions) unidentified. We acquire missing same-site cross-arm information by randomizing participants within selected sites. Under randomized site selection with compatible participant reference distributions and intervention versions, we characterize necessary and sufficient observation patterns for quadratic targets in a model with unrestricted joint distributions of site response means. From finite independent participant samples, we construct unbiased moments and exact covariances. Under regularity conditions, we prove consistency as informative paired site counts grow, allowing fixed within-site sample sizes. For a fixed predictor, we optimize paired-site selection and unequal cell counts using corrected risk variances, pilot error, and costs. In an International Stroke Trial information-deletion experiment, pilot allocation reduces the conditional variance of reconstructing the complete-information corrected risk estimate by 34.3\% relative to uniform allocation with equal expected cost. In 40 Honduras villages, correction reduces estimated residual variation from 0.04081 to 0.00282 in squared log-consumption units for the same fixed explanatory basis; the explained share rises despite a smaller explained component, illustrating how participant sampling noise can inflate estimated residual variation.

title: Improving the Bounds on Approximating Weighted Maximin Share for Chores
authors: Trung Thanh Nguyen and Khaled Elbassioni and J\"{o}rg Rothe
abstract: We investigate the problem of allocating indivisible chores among agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative cost functions. An allocation is said to be $\alpha$-weighted-maximin-share (WMMS) fair if the cost incurred by each agent is at most $\alpha$ times her weighted maximin share. We establish that every instance admits a $4.124234528$-WMMS allocation. Moreover, for instances in which all weights and costs are rational numbers represented in binary, we give an algorithm that computes a $4.12424$-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the total binary encoding length of the input. Complementing these upper bounds, we construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs for which the optimal WMMS approximation factors converge to $e$. Together, our results substantially narrow the previously best-known gap of $[2,12]$ established by Li et al.~\cite{LWX26} to $[e,4.12424]$.

title: Robust Proportionality Axioms for Additive Utilities
abstract: We study the model of participatory budgeting, in which a subset of candidates is selected subject to a budget constraint. Voters express their preferences by assigning a numerical utility to each candidate. Our focus is on formal analysis of proportionality, a central notion of fairness in multi-winner elections. Intuitively, proportionality means that each group of voters should influence the election outcome roughly in proportion to its size. Recent "plus" axioms of proportionality are particularly appealing notions: they are verifiable in polynomial time, and they provide strong representation guarantees without requiring groups of voters to have cohesive preferences. However, their existing formulations are restricted to approval-based preferences. We generalise extended justified representation plus (EJR+), and Core plus (Core+) to general additive utilities. Our approach builds on a payment-based interpretation of proportionality: candidates' costs are shared among their supporters, with the aim of balancing voters' total payments.

title: Lasso Games
abstract: We study games on finite graphs with labelled or weighted edges in which plays end as soon as the first loop is formed. The resulting play has a lasso shape: a path (head) followed by a cycle (loop). We consider two semantics for determining the winner: the loop semantics, where only the loop matters, and the lasso semantics, where the entire play is taken into account. We show that adopting the lasso semantics may have a dramatic impact on both the complexity of the game and the memory required to play optimally. Mean-payoff games with lasso semantics are no longer positionally determined, and the threshold problem â€“ deciding whether the value of the game is at least 0 â€“ is PSPACE-complete. In contrast, lasso parity games are equivalent to weak parity games, remain positionally determined and are solvable in polynomial time. Furthermore, we show that if a positionally determined winning objective is closed under cyclic permutation and both the objective and its complement are closed under concatenation, then it is equivalent to the parity objective. Finally, we consider mod-k games, where the winner depends on the length of the path modulo k >= 2. We show that these games, in both semantics, are PSPACE-complete. Alongside computational complexity, we analyze the memory required to play optimally. We establish that for any game positionally determined in loop semantics, memory of size 2^n is sufficient in lasso semantics. We complement this by showing exponential memory lower bounds for lasso mean-payoff and mod-k games.

title: Representation Theorems for Actual Powers over Two-Agent General Concurrent Game Frames
authors: Thomas {\AA}gotnes (Department of Information Science and Media Studies
abstract: One of the most well-known connections between logic and games is Pauly's representation theorem: the induced powers of individuals and coalitions in concurrent game frames correspond, in a precise sense, to a certain class of neighborhood frames. The precise sense here is what is called alpha effectivity (or alpha power): the power of a coalition is characterized by the sets of states in which it can ensure that the outcome lies by taking some joint action. This definition is inherently monotonic, and, as pointed out by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019), that fact can obscure relevant information about the power structure in the game: we do not know whether two sets that a coalition has the power to enforce correspond to the same joint action or to different joint actions. An alternative is to characterize the power of a coalition by its actual power (called basic power by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019)): the collection of sets of states, each of which corresponds to one joint action by the coalition and all possible joint actions by the other agents. It has recently been argued by Li and Ju (2025, 2026) that standard concurrent game frames rely on three assumptions that may, in some cases, be too strong: seriality, independence of agents, and determinism. This yields a total of eight different classes of general concurrent game frames. In this paper, assuming two agents, we prove that, in terms of actual powers, the eight classes of general concurrent game frames are represented by eight corresponding classes of neighborhood frames. This generalizes a result by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019).

title: Randomized Algorithm for MMS Allocation of Chores with Online Agent Arrivals
authors: Haolong Li and Fangxiao Wang and Xiaowei Wu
abstract: We study the fair allocation of $m$ indivisible chores among $n$ agents in the agent-arrival model against an oblivious adversary. The chore set and the number of agents are known in advance. When agent $i$ arrives, her nonnegative additive cost function $c_i$ is revealed, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably assign her a subset of the unallocated chores. We focus on the notion of maximin share (MMS) and measure the fairness of the realized allocation $X$ by the ex-post MMS approximation ratio $\rho(X)$. We measure an algorithm's performance by its expected ratio, and also the guarantees that hold with high probability. For binary additive costs, we achieve an expected ex-post MMS ratio of $3/2+o(1)$, and show that every randomized online algorithm has an expected ratio of at least $3/2-o(1)$. For every $n$, the expected ratio is at most $1.755$. A variant of our algorithm guarantees an approximation ratio of $2$ with high probability, which is optimal. % For general additive costs, we present a weighted-rounding algorithm that achieves an expected ratio of $2+o(1)$, which also holds with high probability. The expected ratio is at most $2.594$ for every $n$. We also show that similar algorithms extend to additive goods, achieving a constant expected ex-post MMS ratio and guaranteeing every agent an $x$-fraction of her MMS with probability at least $1-85x^2$ for every $x\le1/15$.

title: Polynomial Algorithms for Simultaneous Share-Based and Envy-Based Guarantees
abstract: We study the simultaneous achievement of share-based and envy-based fairness in the allocation of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations. The AnyPrice share (APS) is a strengthening of the maximin share (MMS). A polynomial-time algorithm is known to guarantee a $2n/(3n-1)$ approximation of APS, but without an accompanying envy-based guarantee. Separately, allocations simultaneously satisfying minimum EFX share (MXS) and envy-freeness up to one less-preferred good (EFL), and subsequently the stronger requirement of residual maximin share (RMMS) together with EFL, have been shown to exist. However, the known constructions do not provide pseudopolynomial-time guarantees. We develop algorithms that combine these share-based and envy-based fairness requirements. First, for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we give an algorithm that computes an allocation satisfying exact EFL, $(1-\varepsilon)$-MXS, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Its running time is polynomial in the binary input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Thus, we match the previously established polynomial-time APS approximation while simultaneously guaranteeing exact EFL and an arbitrarily close approximation to MXS. Second, we provide a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously guarantees exact MXS, exact EFL, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Third, for every fixed number of agents, we obtain a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact RMMS and exact EFL. Finally, we establish that computing a numerical threshold between MXS and RMMS is weakly NP-hard, even for additive valuations. This identifies a computational barrier to extending our polynomial-time approach to exact MXS through independently computed residual-valid share thresholds.

title: Deep Neural Mixed Models for Nonlinear Longitudinal Prediction with Subject-Specific Heterogeneity
abstract: Longitudinal health data often exhibit within-subject correlation, subject-specific heterogeneity, and complex nonlinear predictor--response relationships that may not be adequately captured by conventional mixed models. We propose a Deep Generalized Neural Network Mixed Model (DGNMM) that extends the GLMM framework by using a deep neural network to learn nonlinear population-level relationships while incorporating directly trainable, regularized subject-specific effects to capture individual heterogeneity. The model is estimated using prediction-oriented stochastic optimization with separate regularization of the neural-network parameters and subject-specific effects. This formulation allows us to investigate when increased nonlinear representation capacity provides additional predictive benefit in the presence of subject-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study varies population-level nonlinearity and subject-specific heterogeneity and compares DGNMM with GLMM, artificial neural network (ANN), Maity--Pal (MP), and GNMM alternatives for continuous and binary longitudinal outcomes. In the real-data application, DGNMM achieved the lowest MSPE for continuous depression and anxiety prediction, while alternative models remained competitive for binary outcomes. Exploratory subject-level analyses showed heterogeneous predictive gains across individuals, but the magnitude of the estimated subject-specific effects was not significantly associated with predictive gain. Overall, increased nonlinear representation capacity was most beneficial for continuous prediction under nonlinear response structures, while greater subject-specific heterogeneity did not systematically yield larger predictive gains.

title: Online Change-Point Detection in Linear Regression with Autoregressive Errors via Streaming Variational Bayes
abstract: Large-scale streaming time-series regression requires methods that can detect structural changes while accounting for serially correlated errors and quantifying uncertainty about the current regime. We propose a streaming variational Bayes method for linear regression with autoregressive errors that combines online changepoint detection with sequential posterior inference. The proposed method processes observations in chronological mini-batches and uses a finite-mixture variational approximation to represent separate retention and reset configurations for the regression coefficients and innovation variance, while the autoregressive coefficients are shared across regimes and learned sequentially. This construction yields block-specific changepoint probabilities and posterior uncertainty summaries. Closed-form variational updates and mixture pruning enable scalable sequential inference without repeated full-data refits. In simulations, the proposed method maintains low empirical false-alarm rates under stable regimes, with posterior coverage improving as the sample size increases. Under repeated structural changes, it provides accurate type-specific changepoint detection, small changepoint location errors, and short detection delays relative to frequentist sequential monitoring procedures, while posterior coverage approaches nominal levels after an initial adaptation period. An application to high-frequency Bitcoin volatility data illustrates distinct adaptation of the regression and innovation-variance components while accounting for residual autoregressive dependence.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Forecasting Autoregressive Noncausal Processes
abstract: This paper examines the use of recurrent neural networks and their extensions for forecasting autoregressive causal-noncausal processes, characterized by local explosive patterns such as bubbles and spikes. We study the recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), gated recurrent unit (GRU), bidirectional LSTM, and also a simple feed-forward network (FNN) to reveal the difficulty of forecasting extreme values depending on the type of network and the length of the training set. We show that FNN outperforms other networks in predicting extreme values of a univariate noncausal time series during a bubble. We also examine the improvements of point predictions of extreme values resulting from pooling and a modified loss function.

title: Approximation, Consistency, and Prediction in Generalized Neural Network Mixed Models for Longitudinal and Clustered Data
abstract: Generalized neural network mixed models (GNMMs) combine neural networks and mixed-effects models to analyze longitudinal and clustered data. Although GNMMs have shown good predictive performance in practice, their statistical properties are not well understood. Therefore, this paper studies several important properties of GNMM and provides theoretical support for its use. First, we show that the neural-network component can approximate an unknown nonlinear fixed-effect function arbitrarily well and establish consistency of the fitted neural- network function for its population target within a given network class. Next, we establish consistency of random-effect estimation under increasing within-subject information and show that the GNMM predictor converges to the true predictor. We then prove consistency of the conditional mean function and show that the excess mean squared prediction error (MSPE) relative to the oracle prediction error converges to zero. We conduct simulation studies to examine nonlinear fixed-effect recovery, random-effect estimation, predictor and conditional mean estimation, and excess prediction error under different numbers of subjects and repeated observations. We also apply GNMM to a longitudinal schizophrenia dataset to predict continuous and binary depression outcomes using smartphone- based behavioral measurements and compare its predictive performance with generalized linear mixed models and conventional artificial neural networks. Both the theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that GNMM provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear longitudinal and clustered data. These findings provide a statistical foundation for GNMM prediction and support future methodological developments.

title: Moment-Calibrated Conformal Prediction with Side Information
abstract: For a fixed conformal score function, standard split conformal prediction calibrates a prediction set using the empirical distribution of the conformal scores, without using available side information about the data. We propose a moment-calibrated approach that uses such information to reduce variability across calibration data sets. Side information involving the covariates, the response, or both is expressed as moment restrictions, which are enforced through empirical likelihood weights on the calibration data points. The resulting weighted empirical distribution of the scores determines the weighted empirical quantile without changing the score function. We establish finite-sample bounds on training-conditional and marginal coverage of the moment-calibrated prediction set. We derive asymptotic distributions for training-conditional coverage and average prediction-set size, show that their asymptotic variances are no larger than the corresponding variances under standard split conformal prediction, and characterize when the reductions are strict. In the semi-supervised setting, we identify an optimal moment function of a given covariate representation, develop implementations using prespecified moment functions or a function learned by cross-fitting, and quantify the effect of the unlabeled sample size. We also extend the method to coverage conditions indexed by a class of functions of the covariates through weighted quantile regression. Numerical studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

title: Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market
abstract: EIP-4844 gave Ethereum rollups a separate fee dimension for data, governed by a multiplicative update rule that targets three ``blobs'' per block. Whether this target is reached depends on how many independent, self-interested rollups choose to post data, a question that closed-form models address only for a single agent under exogenous prices or in a static equilibrium. We propose a calibrated multi-agent reinforcement learning environment for the blob fee market in which the blob base fee is endogenous, set by the EIP-4844 rule on the aggregated decisions of heterogeneous rollups fit to post-Dencun Ethereum data. After confirming that the environment reproduces the known single-agent analytical optimum, we show that independent learners, with no convergence guarantee, still settle near the target without coordination ($3.32\pm0.01$ blobs per block over five seeds). Over a fiftyfold demand range ($10\times$ to $500\times$), supply stays at the target from $10\times$ to $200\times$ and rises above it at higher demand, where the fee can no longer hold it. Posting frequency increases with rollup size, an emergent analog of the size threshold predicted by prior theory. A costless layer-1 calldata outside option pushes the fee down by roughly an order of magnitude while aggregate supply stays at the target, so the fee rule acts as a negative-feedback controller on decentralized supply.

title: Stable Causal Estimation with Optimal Transport
abstract: In observational studies, the overlap assumption, also called positivity, is frequently strained in practice. Limited overlap destabilizes widely used estimators such as inverse propensity weighting (IPW), whose variance depends on density ratios that explode as propensity scores approach zero or one. To address this challenge, we propose the Stable Transport Estimator (STE), an optimal transport-based approach for estimating average causal effects when overlap holds but strict overlap fails. Unlike IPW, the variance of STE contains no density-ratio factor; it is governed by the transport map itself and stays finite under bounded moments, even when density ratios diverge. By replacing reweighting with a geometry-aware transport map, STE constructs stable counterfactual comparisons without requiring density estimation or propensity score modeling. STE further extends to settings where the overlap condition is violated: when covariate supports overlap only partially, a linear interpolation transport map enables principled extrapolation with explicit bias-variance trade-offs. We establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and a variance characterization that makes explicit the contribution of the estimated transport map to the asymptotic variance. Across synthetic and real datasets, STE demonstrates improved robustness, reduced bias, and markedly more stable variance compared to existing estimators.

title: Precision follows the decision: how well an acceptance probability is known for mean-spread release rules
abstract: Many release rules accept a lot when a statistic built from the sample mean and standard deviation stays within a limit, and the probability that a process passes such a rule can be computed exactly for a broad class of parent distributions. This paper asks how well that probability is itself known once the parent has been estimated. Under a stated reference posterior the answer is an interval, narrow where a lot clearly passes or fails and wide where it is contested. In ninety-eight published content-uniformity lots that position, not the sample size, sets the width: among the forty-eight lots assayed at the same ten units, and so equally informed about the spread, the $95\%$ interval runs from essentially zero width to $0.96$. With the operating point held fixed while test and estimation sample grow together, the interval narrows only slowly, the contraction of the posterior being offset by the steepening of the operating characteristic; a calibrated study at the sample sizes of $1207$ occupational exposure assessments shows the same under a half-plane rule. For a pure-spread rule under a Normal parent the interval has an exact chi-square form in the plug-in value and the two sample sizes, extending to the mean-spread wedge with a measured residual and containing Bergum's lower bound as one endpoint. With the parent's posterior formed from the same published summaries through the evaluator's own likelihood, the qualitative pattern survives but shape moves both endpoints and width: on the same lots a strong right skew lowers the pessimistic endpoint by up to a fifth and widens the interval by up to $0.22$. At the content-uniformity operating point studied, under a Normal parent, the symmetric error bar in standard use puts the lower endpoint $0.21$ too high and returns an upper endpoint above one, even with the full posterior covariance.

title: Closed forms all the way up: the sample variance of four observations
abstract: The distribution function $F(y)=\Pr(S^2\le y)$ of the sample variance $S^2$ of four independent observations is elementary on its entire support for every polynomial parent density on $[0,1]$ (without loss of generality), and we give it in finite closed form for the uniform, Beta$(2,1)$ and Beta$(2,2)$ parents. The support splits at $y = 1/6$, $2/9$ and $1/4$, with the ceiling at $1/3$, all fixed by geometry: in coordinates aligned with the cube diagonal the event $S^2\le y$ is a ball of radius $\sqrt{3y}$, the cube projects to a rhombic dodecahedron, and these are the levels at which the ball reaches its faces, edges and two kinds of vertices. The divergence theorem reduces every moment of the clipped ball to integrals along circular arcs, so each regime closes in algebraic functions of $\sqrt{y}$ and inverse trigonometric functions. For the uniform parent the only non-obvious constant is $K_g = 12\sqrt2\arctan\sqrt2$, proportional to the mean width of the cuboctahedron; the Beta constants are rational expressions in $\pi$, $\sqrt2$, $\sqrt3$ and $\arctan\sqrt2$, as in the uniform case. At $n = 4$ the normal-theory $\chi^2$ recipe used in acceptance testing misplaces the $99$th percentile of $S^2$ by $50\%$ for the uniform parent. For three observations, polynomial parents also give elementary closed forms (arXiv:2609.25333), but two elementary cases in a row do not guarantee a third, and we make no claim beyond $n = 4$.

title: GMM under finite-population asymptotics: instrumental variables and regression adjustment
abstract: This paper extends the finite-population asymptotic framework of Abadie et al. (2014,2020) to the generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator for moment condition models. Motivating examples include instrumental variable regressions and regression adjustments under randomized controlled trials. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the GMM estimator and propose conservative variance estimators. We also study GMM weighting, misspecification, and over-identification testing under finite-population asymptotics. Notably, even though the optimally weighted GMM estimator is infeasible under finite-population asymptotics, the regression adjustment estimator in a randomized controlled trial is shown to be asymptotically equivalent to the optimally weighted GMM estimator. A simulation study and real data application illustrate the usefulness of our GMM theory.

title: A Cosine-Projection Framework for Choosing Among Cox HR, D-RMST, and Average-Hazard Tests in Survival Trials
abstract: The log-rank/Cox hazard-ratio test remains the standard approach for the primary analysis of randomized trials with time-to-event endpoints and is fully efficient under proportional hazards (PH). Two model-free alternatives that have recently gained attention are the difference in restricted mean survival time (D-RMST), a contrast on the time scale, and the more recently proposed ratio of average hazards (RAH), a contrast on the rate scale. Simulation studies suggest that the RAH-based test can outperform both under delayed treatment effects, but its efficiency has not been characterized analytically, and no unified framework explains how censoring and accrual affect the efficiency ordering among these tests. We show that all three statistics share a weighted-log-rank representation and derive their asymptotic relative efficiencies under local alternatives, including the first analytic efficiency results for the RAH-based test. Geometrically, each test defines a direction in a function space and the anticipated treatment effect defines a signal direction. A test's efficiency relative to the oracle test equals the squared cosine of the angle between these directions, so the asymptotic relative efficiency of any two tests is a ratio of squared cosines. Because censoring and accrual enter through an information weight, the framework shows how design choices can alter, and even reverse, the efficiency ordering. We illustrate the framework using the CheckMate 057 immunotherapy trial and corroborate the theoretical results through simulations spanning proportional- and non-proportional-hazards settings.

title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

title: Coalition-Proof Disclosure
abstract: We study generalized verifiable disclosure by a sender with type-independent preferences. We first characterize all perfect Bayesian equilibria as partitions of the sender's types into coalitions ordered by payoff. An equilibrium survives our coalition-proofness criterion if no group of types can profitably coordinate an announced deviation that only they are able and willing to join. Coalition-proof equilibria are greedy partitions: at each step, a coalition of the remaining types attains the highest payoff consistent with equilibrium. In our general setting, coalition-proof equilibria may fail to exist. We establish existence under restrictions on preferences and evidence: quasiconcavity with message completeness, betweenness, cheap talk with message completeness, and payoff degradation. For a disclosure game with maximally rich evidence, we show that the sender's ex-ante payoff in a coalition-proof equilibrium is a piecewise linear tent over the belief simplex, analogous to the concave closure in Bayesian persuasion and the quasiconcave closure in cheap talk.

title: A model-assisted design for phase I oncology drug combination trials incorporating backfill
authors: Connor Celum (1) and Evan M. Bagley (2 and 3) ((1) Statistics Department
abstract: Historically, phase I oncology trials were designed with the focus to find the highest tolerable dose. However, given the FDA's acknowledgment that the highest tolerable dose might not be the dose which is optimal biologically, there is an increased emphasis the development of designs that explore the dose-toxicity and dose-efficacy relationship. Backfill designs have emerged as a popular response to address this need by allocating participants to doses deemed safe while awaiting participants outcomes. Previous designs have explored how to assign participants to doses in backfill designs in a rigorous manner while providing simplicity and performance (a class of designs known as model-assisted) for single agents. Still, a research gap exists in the lack of model-assisted backfill designs for drug combinations. Frequently, the combinations two of cancer agents are explored in phase I trials, with the goal of identifying the highest tolerable combination. This paper incorporates and extends methodology based on previous model-assisted backfill designs to provide clinicians with a simple-to-use backfill design for phase I drug combination trials.

title: Randomized Experiments with Ambiguous Record Linkage
abstract: Randomized experiments are often linked to administrative data to measure outcomes, but coarse identifiers can leave multiple administrative records consistent with each experimental unit. We show that unbiased estimation of the sample average treatment effect is possible without resolving these ambiguous links or specifying an outcome model. Our key linkage requirement is that the true administrative outcome is contained among the candidate outcomes for each experimental unit. We characterize the precision cost of linkage ambiguity and study two complementary ways to mitigate it: regression adjustment and reweighting based on observed linkage characteristics. We establish finite-sample and asymptotic properties of these estimators and develop valid randomization-based and large-sample inference.

title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
abstract: Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two-dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co-player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co-player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long-term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always-defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit-for-tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.

title: Rate-Based Causal Discovery for Heavy-Tailed Models
abstract: In many complex systems, such as river networks and financial markets, extreme events propagate from causes to their effects, and the largest observations carry the most information about the underlying causal structure. Existing methods for causal discovery in extremes, however, are tailored to specific mechanisms, such as linear or max-linear models. This work develops causal discovery for heavy-tailed homogeneous structural causal models, a flexible class that contains linear, max-linear and norm-type mechanisms, which may differ from node to node. In these models, the causal structure is encoded by ancestral impulse responses, which measure how a shock at one node is transmitted to its descendants. We propose the extremal minimum ratio estimator of these responses, which uses only observations in which the potential cause is extreme. The estimator is consistent under regular variation alone, and we derive its exact rates of convergence and limiting distributions, which depend on both the causal relation and the type of mechanism. Building on these rates, we construct consistent estimators of the causal order and of the full set of ancestral relations, using a threshold that adapts to the data and requires no knowledge of the tail index. The method is illustrated on simulated data and on river discharges in the upper Danube basin.

title: Recurrent Barycenter Encoder: Prediction, Simulation and Applications to Time Series Analysis
abstract: This dissertation has two parts. In the first part we theoretically develop a framework that extends the optimal transport barycenter problem from independent data with observed covariates to processes whose relevant covariate is their own history. Given a stationary stochastic process, our framework shows there exists an invertible transport map that extracts from it an iid component whose distribution is the barycenter of the conditional distributions of the input process on its own past. This extracted iid sequence thus captures the innovation or noise component of the process that is not explained by the process's own past. In the second part of this thesis we implement an effective algorithm to solve this problem and test it against synthetic data generated with some well-known models in time series analysis for which the solution is known in closed-form. We then show how this method can be applied to build a predictive sampler for such processes, and assess the accuracy of this predictive sampler both with the aforementioned synthetic data and with real-world time series such as the S&P 500 and Bitcoin 4-hour returns, and the daily records of the North Atlantic Oscillation index from the NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Finally, we demonstrate an application of the sampler to path simulation with a well-known time series model.

title: Can You Trust Your Preference Models? Stackelberg Games for Alignment
authors: Riccardo Formenti and Aditya Agrawal and Vikas Garg
abstract: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. We formulate this search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between two opposing policies, a Leader which tries to minimize disagreement, and a Follower which maximizes it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games, we establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness and a closed-form characterization. We introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (SMIDA), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting, and develop a neural policy-gradient analogue. Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error. On held out data the trained policies outperform reference policies and increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.

title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves
abstract: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn't trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.

title: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Division via Subsidies
abstract: We study the relationship between fair division with $\textit{subsidies}$ and $\textit{best-of-both-worlds}$ (BoBW) fairness for indivisible items. We prove a general reduction of BoBW existence to envy-freeability. Specifically, for any scale-free ex-post property $P$ (e.g., EF1, EFX, PO) and any scale-free valuation class $\mathcal{V}$ (e.g, additive, submodular, subadditive, monotone), if every instance in $\mathcal{V}$ admits a $P$-allocation that can be made envy-free using subsidies, then every such instance admits an ex-ante envy-free lottery supported on $P$-allocations. The proof uses linear programming duality. As applications, the reduction gives alternative proofs of BoBW existence results for additive goods, chores, and mixtures of goods and chores. The converse of our general reduction holds for two agents but fails for three: We provide a four-good counterexample with monotone submodular valuations where an ex-ante envy-free and ex-post EF1 lottery exists, but no allocation is simultaneously EF1 and envy-freeable. For lexicographic valuations, we prove simultaneous EFX, Pareto optimality, and envy-freeability (and hence BoBW guarantees for EFX+PO) for three agents, and show that even EFX and envy-freeability can be incompatible for four agents.

title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
abstract: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.

title: Allocative Efficiency and the Returns to Innovation
abstract: Innovation changes welfare through the technology it adds and the reallocation it causes between producers with different markups. When producers set markups, an innovator's own output and price adjustments have no private value at the margin, so reallocation reaches its profit only through others' responses. For an innovator small in its markets, none of the change in allocative efficiency, which is of the same order as its cost saving, reaches its profit under quantity or price competition. A process innovator is paid its cost saving, forgoing its own and downstream markups on added output. For U.S. public firms in 2015, these average 14 to 26 percent of that saving, and allocative efficiency rises or falls by more than a tenth of the private return for innovators holding 56 percent of sales. With estimated spillovers, patenting firms' R&D has a social return 6.24 times its private return.

title: An Algebraic Approach to Constrained K-means Clustering
abstract: Clustering is typically performed using only object features, although additional information about relationships between objects may be available and can be incorporated through constraints. Among these, pairwise constraints require two objects to belong to the same cluster or to different clusters. Several extensions of the k-means algorithm accommodate such constraints, but they sometimes fail to find a feasible assignment or incur high computational cost. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an algebraic approach to k-means clustering with pairwise constraints. The algorithm simplifies the constraints using Gr\"{o}bner bases before optimization, improving the efficiency of cluster assignment. It can also detect whether the constraint set has a feasible assignment before optimization. Comparative experiments with existing algorithms showed that the proposed algorithm achieved comparable or better clustering quality at a lower computational cost, particularly when the numbers of constraints and clusters were small.

title: Multilateral governance of invasive alien species management: An ecological-economic model with Allee effect
abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) generate substantial ecological and economic damages that often transcend political boundaries, creating strong incentives for coordinated management. We develop a two-region ecological-economic model of IAS control that integrates prevention and eradication measures with population dynamics characterized by logistic growth and an Allee effect. We derive analytical results on the interaction between ecological thresholds and strategic behaviour and compare outcomes under cooperation (central planner) and non-cooperation (open loop Nash equilibrium and Markovian Nash equilibrium). We show that, under realistic control costs, neither prevention nor eradication can eliminate invasive populations in finite time, and complete prevention of cross-border spread is generally not optimal. In the absence of an Allee effect, the zero-population equilibrium is unstable, implying long-run persistence of the invasive species. By contrast, the presence of an Allee effect fundamentally alters system dynamics by making extinction locally stable and creating a basin of attraction within which eradication becomes feasible. This finding highlights the economic significance of ecological thresholds and demonstrates how delays in management can shift populations beyond critical levels, after which eradication is unlikely regardless of subsequent control efforts. Numerical simulations further show that cooperative management expands the set of initial conditions leading to eradication and consistently reduces aggregate social costs relative to decentralized management. The results provide a formal rationale for rapid intervention, precautionary regulation, and stronger multilateral cooperation in IAS management, particularly in jurisdictions such as the European Union where listing and control actions may be delayed pending evidence of harm.

title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents
abstract: Language models are increasingly used to create synthetic survey samples, also called silicon samples. Decision models are a new class of language models that return a probability for each point of a rating scale instead of text. We ask whether these models, or the newest generative LLMs, can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. We test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey (n=263, 68 items), with 100 real respondent profiles, the Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) and statistical baselines. The best generative model, MiniMax M3, reaches PSS 0.813. This is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.824) and below a copula fit in sample (0.927). A second sample of 100 real people scores below the best models, so at this size PSS cannot rank them against real respondents. In 5 of 10 product lines the newest generative release scores below an earlier release of the same line beyond resampling noise, and none gains beyond it. With the default rounded readout, 13 of 14 decision models score below the generative reference gpt-5.4-mini. Of the 47 generative models, 33 reproduce the pattern of item correlations better than any decision model. Averaged over respondents, the probability vectors are much closer to the human item marginals than rounded answers. They also rank respondents about as well as a profile regression fit on 163 real people. As forecasts of each person's own answers, however, every decision model is worse than the answer frequencies of other respondents, mainly because its average vector differs from them. The profile regression improves on these frequencies by only 1.0%, so the profile fields say little about how a person answers. Synthetic respondents built on such profiles should therefore aim at sample-level fidelity.

title: Comparing randomized trials
authors: Yu-Han Chiu and Issa J. Dahabreh
abstract: Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.

title: Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market
abstract: We build a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers: they apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. Firms post vacancies, workers search with friction, and product demand slopes downward. Across 30 seeded runs per configuration, AI entry at 70% of the human wage raises unemployment by 4.1 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 4.6) and leaves 12.2 fewer humans employed (CI 10.5 to 13.9). Layoffs dominate when AI is much cheaper than humans: the layoff margin accounts for 7.2 of the lost jobs and reduced hiring for 5.0, though most dismissed workers find work again. A wider price gap reduces displacement, because cheap AI makes firms expand: at price parity, with zero dismissals, the unemployment effect is largest at 9.2 points (CI 8.6 to 9.9), all of it through hiring. That parity result survives cutting AI applications from five per period to one. Demand elasticity decides how many workers AI displaces. Screening changes who gets hired and leaves the displacement total unchanged.

title: An Unscented PrO Kalman Filter
abstract: Predictively-oriented (PrO) filtering for state-space models was proposed in Shen et al. [2026] as a promising route to avoiding over-confident inferences in settings where either the dynamical model, the measurement model, or both, could be misspecified. Our focus is on nonlinear state-space models, where the local linearisation used to construct the PrO filter in Shen et al. [2026] deteriorates as nonlinearities enter either the dynamical model or the measurement model. Our proposed solution is based on unscented transforms, an established tool from classical filtering which provides a more accurate mechanism to propagate Gaussian uncertainty through a nonlinear functional, and which includes the cubature rule as a special case. We introduce two variants: replacing the linearisation in the predict step alone, which we call UKF-PrO, has a computational cost comparable to the existing PrO filter; replacing it in the update step as well, UKF-PrO+, requires a substantially more expensive joint optimisation. Performance is empirically assessed on the Lorenz96 model under conditions of increasing difficulty, in which the state-space model is systematically misspecified; we find that UKF-PrO with the parameters of the cubature Kalman filter offers consistent improvements, which become substantial under strong nonlinearity, whereas the default unscented parameters are unreliable, and that the full update-step extension with the same parameters does not justify its additional cost.

title: The price of a weak shadow variable: inference under nonignorable missingness as relevance vanishes
abstract: When an outcome is missing not at random, identification is commonly restored by a shadow variable: a covariate that predicts the outcome but is excluded from the response mechanism. The literature treats the first requirement, relevance, as a yes-or-no condition. We make it continuous, parametrizing it by a scalar that scales the shadow variable's entire contribution to the moment conditions, and ask what inference costs as that scalar vanishes. One functional of the inverse weight governs the answer. We characterize it exactly, show that it fixes the effective sample size, and use it to sharpen the rates of the estimator that avoids the weight. The characterization is concrete. Whether the functional saturates or diverges turns not on boundedness of the outcome but on whether the tilting variable has an atom at its essential supremum: a binary outcome saturates, a uniform one does not. It also bounds how far a scanned set reaches, and that reach grows only as the square root of the logarithm of the sample size, so a thousandfold increase buys one unit of tilt while the set to be scanned widens. A reanalyzed credit-scoring study shows the cost: a characteristic an optimizing selector uses cannot satisfy exclusion.

title: Beyond Independent Values: Optimal Auctions with Correlated Valuations for LLM-Native Advertising
abstract: Conversational assistants are becoming the place where people ask what to buy, and sponsored content is moving into their answers. Several advertisers then compete for one sponsored slot, and all of them read the same conversation, so their willingness to pay usually moves together. Existing auctions for LLM advertising treat these values as independent. We therefore present AffMyerson, an auction that captures this correlation and turns it into revenue. We model the advertisers' values given the conversation as a multivariate normal and turn the economic premise of positive dependence (affiliation) into a sign condition on the precision matrix. We design a neural parameterization whose every output satisfies it. We prove that every prior in this family yields a truthful, ex-post individually rational auction, so estimation error can cost revenue but never truthfulness. We derive the conditional virtual values in closed form. By the design of the prior, pricing an auction needs no matrix inversion and takes O(n^2) time, fast enough to run at query time. We also work out the log-normal family used in empirical ad-auction work. There we prove that the auction is truthful for every prior and revenue-optimal when the prior is correct, and that the virtual value is regular everywhere whenever the conditional spread is below a loose threshold, which our fitted priors stay well under. With LLM-agent bidders, AffMyerson earns 6.2% more than a second-price auction with a tuned reserve, 6.1% more than Ronen's lookahead auction with the same prior, and 9.2% more than Myerson's auction run as if values were independent. This gain is still 4.5% on real keyword search queries where willingness to pay is hard to read. The correlation comes from common demand. Agents that judge the conversation bid together and agents told to calculate do not. The gain from conditioning moves with the correlation.

title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels
abstract: Human reference labels used to evaluate medical AI can vary across readers and annotation workflows. We quantified agreement of a fixed pathology AI system with a future qualified reader without treating inferred consensus as error-free biological truth. Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data were analyzed using a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. The selected frame contained 1,144 anchors, 52 fields of view, five slides/patients, and five primary readers. The target was fixed-AI agreement with a future reader, with descriptive contrast $\Delta=\theta_E-\theta_U$. Analyses included raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment. Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs observed in both conditions, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state, while raw agreement was 0.5466 in Unbiased and 0.5473 in Evaluation. The reader-only model gave $\Delta=-0.0008$ (95% CrI, $-0.0033$ to $0.0008$), and the shared-detectability model gave $\Delta\approx0$ ($-0.0140$ to $0.0127$). Across structural perturbations, absolute agreement ranged from 0.420 to 0.646 in Unbiased and 0.409 to 0.640 in Evaluation. Frozen adversarial simulations met the comparative-stability criterion (median $R=0.295$; 14/16 model-scenario cells had $R<1$). Held-out-AI prediction supported shared predictive information, but varied by slide composition. The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast was comparatively stable, whereas absolute agreement was structurally sensitive. These findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or new-patient transportability. Evaluations using variable human references should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.

title: From Observation to Intervention: Mastering Bus Holding Control from Historical Uncontrolled Trajectories with Offline Reinforcement Learning
